title: Stage 3: Contract and validation
summary: Publish the contract, validate before calling any backend, and accept orders.

steps.title: Stage 3: contract first
body: - `GET /api/openapi.json` serves the API's OpenAPI contract (a raw string literal is fine) with the operations
contract first) and `createOrder` (`POST /api/orders`). It stays public in later stages: documentation needs no token.
- `GET /api/books/{isbn}` validates the ISBN against the pattern **before** calling the backend. Invalid →
- not JSON → `400` with details `["body: is not valid JSON"]`;
- otherwise collect **every** problem, in this order: `isbn: is required` / `isbn: does not match ^97[89][0-9]{10}$`;
`quantity: is required` / `quantity: expected integer` / `quantity: must be between 1 and 10`;
`email: is required` / `email: is not an email address` (pattern `^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+$`);
- valid → `POST /backend/orders` with **only** `isbn`, `quantity` and `email` (extra fields are dropped), then

steps.prompt: The gateway will validate requests against the contract in a later stage. Why validate in the integration as well?
options: The integration builds the backend URL from the ISBN; it must never send garbage, whatever the gateway did
Because the gateway can't read JSON
It shouldn't; validation belongs only at the gateway
steps.explain: Defence in depth: each layer protects what it is responsible for.

lines: Validate every field and collect all problems
Send only the contract's fields to the order backend
Map a backend failure to the error contract
201 with the orderId and a Location header

steps.prompt: A consumer sends `{"isbn":"123","quantity":50}`. Why return all three problems at once instead of stopping at the first?
options: The consumer can fix everything in one round trip instead of discovering problems one at a time
It is faster for the server
To hide which field was wrong
